papers.title: "It Listens Better Than My Therapist": Exploring Social Media Discourse on LLMs as Mental Health Tool
papers.abstract: The emergence of generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT has prompted growing public and academic interest in their role as informal mental health support tools. While early rule-based systems have been around for several years, large language models (LLMs) offer new capabilities in conversational fluency, empathy simulation, and availability. This study explores how users engage with LLMs as mental health tools by analyzing over 10,000 TikTok comments from videos referencing LLMs as mental health tools. Using a self-developed tiered coding schema and supervised classification models, we identify user experiences, attitudes, and recurring themes. Results show that nearly 20% of comments reflect personal use, with these users expressing overwhelmingly positive attitudes. Commonly cited benefits include accessibility, emotional support, and perceived therapeutic value. However, concerns around privacy, generic responses, and the lack of professional oversight remain prominent. It is important to note that the user feedback does not indicate which therapeutic framework, if any, the LLM-generated output aligns with. While the findings underscore the growing relevance of AI in everyday practices, they also highlight the urgent need for clinical and ethical scrutiny in the use of AI for mental health support.

papers.title: Foundations of GenIR
papers.abstract: The chapter discusses the foundational impact of modern generative AI models on information access (IA) systems. In contrast to traditional AI, the large-scale training and superior data modeling of generative AI models enable them to produce high-quality, human-like responses, which brings brand new opportunities for the development of IA paradigms. In this chapter, we identify and introduce two of them in details, i.e., information generation and information synthesis. Information generation allows AI to create tailored content addressing user needs directly, enhancing user experience with immediate, relevant outputs. Information synthesis leverages the ability of generative AI to integrate and reorganize existing information, providing grounded responses and mitigating issues like model hallucination, which is particularly valuable in scenarios requiring precision and external knowledge. This chapter delves into the foundational aspects of generative models, including architecture, scaling, and training, and discusses their applications in multi-modal scenarios. Additionally, it examines the retrieval-augmented generation paradigm and other methods for corpus modeling and understanding, demonstrating how generative AI can enhance information access systems. It also summarizes potential challenges and fruitful directions for future studies.

papers.title: Reframing Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Care: Toward a Human-Centered, Explainable, and Clinically Responsible Psychotherapeutic Paradigm
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Mental Health care represents a transformative shift in the diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of psychological disorders. While AI-driven tools—including digital phenotyping systems, natural language processing models, and conversational agents—offer significant potential to enhance diagnostic precision, accessibility, and personalized interventions, they simultaneously introduce complex ethical, clinical, and epistemological challenges. This study provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of contemporary literature (2019–2025) to examine the ethical implications of AI deployment in psychotherapeutic contexts. Moving beyond descriptive review, the paper develops a conceptual ethical governance framework grounded in the principles of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice, as well as the emerging “ethics of care” paradigm. It identifies key risk domains, including algorithmic bias, opacity of decision-making processes, data privacy vulnerabilities, erosion of therapeutic alliance, and the reconfiguration of professional accountability. Furthermore, the study proposes a human-centered, explainable, and clinically supervised AI integration model, emphasizing transparency, continuous ethical auditing, stakeholder inclusion, and hybrid human–AI decision-making structures. The findings highlight that while AI can significantly improve efficiency and expand access to mental healthcare—particularly in resource-constrained settings—its unregulated or poorly designed application may exacerbate inequalities, compromise patient autonomy, and undermine trust in clinical practice. The paper contributes to the interdisciplinary discourse by offering a structured ethical framework that bridges technological innovation with clinical responsibility and humanistic values. It concludes that sustainable and ethically aligned AI integration in mental health requires robust regulatory architectures, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and the preservation of the fundamentally human dimensions of psychotherapy.

papers.title: A Systematic Review on Artificial Intelligence-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems in Depression
papers.abstract: Purpose: This systematic review examines the current landscape of artificial intelligence (AI)-based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) designed to aid in the treatment of depression. With depression recognized as a complex and multifactorial condition, often differing across contexts such as postpartum, adolescence, and elderly populations, the review aims to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and potential of AI-based CDSS in supporting personalized care. The primary research question explores how these systems are implemented and evaluated in clinical settings, as well as the main challenges to their broader adoption.Methods: The review analyzed studies focused on AI-based CDSS for depression, identifying variations in algorithms, performance metrics, and implementations. Studies were assessed based on system purposes, categorized into treatment selection, prediction and risk assessment, and clinical support and data review, providing a comprehensive overview of each study’s approach and outcomes.Results: 11 unique algorithms, 9 performance metrics, and 10 CDSS implementations were identified across the studies. Findings indicate positive results for CDSS in supporting clinical decision-making, yet highlight challenges in applying these tools in routine practice. Limitations include small, non-diverse sample sizes, immature methodologies, and difficulties in workflow integration, along with concerns about data privacy and the ethical use of AI.Conclusions: AI-based CDSS for depression shows potential in patient care; however, foundational issues such as more diverse samples and robust model development remain critical. Addressing these aspects will set the stage for future research into advanced applications, such as virtual-reality integration and multi-condition prediction, thus advancing AI’s role in mental health treatment.Clinical Relevance—This work illustrates the state of art of AI adoption in the domain of mental health, specifically in the context of depression.

papers.title: The application of AI-assisted music therapy tools in mental health interventions
papers.abstract: With the rising prevalence of mental health problems across populations, the limitations of traditional interventions have become more evident. Music therapy has received growing attention as a psychological intervention, and recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new opportunities for this field. This review examines the application potential and implementation pathways of AI-assisted music therapy tools for mental health interventions. Drawing on the literature and representative cases, this review summarizes application models and reported effects of AI in music therapy. The available evidence suggests that AI-assisted music therapy tools can support personalized interventions by adapting to users’ emotional and psychological states. Reported benefits include reductions in anxiety and depressive symptoms and improvements in emotion regulation across groups such as children, adolescents, and older adults. Finally, this review outlines priorities for future translation into mental health services and emphasizes data privacy and ethical standards to ensure responsible deployment.

literature_themes.theme: AI in Mental Health: User Perspectives, Clinical Systems, and Ethical Governance
literature_themes.summary: This cluster examines the use of AI, particularly LLMs and CDSS, in mental health support. Paper 1 analyzes social media discourse, finding positive user attitudes towards LLMs for emotional support but concerns about privacy and lack of professional oversight. Paper 4 reviews AI-based CDSS for depression, identifying various algorithms and implementations with positive results for treatment support. Paper 3 proposes an ethical governance framework for AI in mental health, highlighting risks like bias and erosion of therapeutic alliance. Paper 5 explores AI-assisted music therapy tools, showing benefits in reducing anxiety and depression across populations.
literature_themes.limitations: Key limitations include: lack of clinical validation and professional oversight (Paper 1), variability in algorithms and performance metrics (Paper 4), unresolved ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias and data privacy (Paper 3), and need for more rigorous studies on AI-music therapy efficacy (Paper 5).
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights gaps in: understanding long-term therapeutic outcomes of AI tools, integrating user feedback into clinical system design, developing explainable and ethical AI frameworks, and bridging the gap between informal AI use and formal clinical practice. These gaps can inform research on responsible AI deployment in mental health.

literature_themes.summary: This cluster examines the foundational impact of generative AI on information access systems, focusing on two key paradigms: information generation (creating tailored content) and information synthesis (integrating existing knowledge). It covers generative model architecture, scaling, training, and applications in multi-modal scenarios, including retrieval-augmented generation.
literature_themes.limitations: The cluster primarily discusses conceptual foundations and opportunities, with limited empirical validation or comparative analysis against traditional IR methods. Issues like model hallucination are mentioned but not deeply addressed in terms of mitigation strategies.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the need for robust evaluation frameworks for generative IR, and underscores gaps in handling hallucination, grounding, and precision in knowledge-intensive tasks. It can support gap identification by pointing to under-explored areas such as multi-modal generative IR and scalable training for domain-specific applications.

summary: The literature reveals that AI tools, including LLMs and CDSS, are increasingly used in mental health support, showing benefits in accessibility and symptom reduction but raising concerns about privacy, bias, and lack of clinical oversight. Ethical frameworks emphasize human-centered, explainable, and supervised integration, while gaps remain in long-term outcomes, user feedback integration, and robust evaluation. Foundational work on generative IR highlights potential for tailored content and knowledge synthesis, though challenges like hallucination persist. Overall, responsible deployment requires addressing ethical, clinical, and technical limitations.
gap: How can user feedback from informal AI mental health tools (e.g., LLMs) be systematically integrated into the design of clinically validated, ethical AI systems to improve therapeutic outcomes and user trust?
question: How can user feedback from informal AI mental health tools (e.g., LLMs) be systematically integrated into the design of clinically validated, ethical AI systems to improve therapeutic outcomes and user trust?
hypothesis: Integrating user feedback from informal LLM interactions into a structured feedback loop for a clinically supervised CDSS will improve treatment adherence and user trust compared to a CDSS without such feedback integration.
methodology: A mixed-methods study with two phases. Phase 1: Thematic analysis of user feedback from social media (e.g., TikTok comments) on LLM-based mental health tools, coding for benefits, concerns, and suggestions. Phase 2: Co-design workshops with clinicians, AI developers, and users to translate themes into design requirements for a CDSS. The CDSS will be prototyped and evaluated in a small-scale pilot RCT (n=60) comparing a feedback-informed CDSS vs. standard CDSS, measuring adherence, trust (Likert scale), and symptom reduction (PHQ-9/GAD-7) at 4 weeks.
proposal: AI tools like LLMs and CDSS show promise in mental health but lack systematic integration of user feedback from informal platforms into clinically validated systems, as highlighted by gaps in user-centered design (Papers 1, 3, 4) and underutilization of generative IR for feedback synthesis (Paper 2). This study asks: How can user feedback from informal LLM interactions be systematically integrated into a clinically supervised CDSS to improve therapeutic outcomes and user trust? We hypothesize that a feedback-informed CDSS, using a structured feedback loop based on the Double Diamond design process, will improve adherence and trust over a standard CDSS. A mixed-methods design includes: Phase 1 – thematic analysis of TikTok comments (n=500) using grounded theory with inter-coder reliability (Cohen's κ>0.8); Phase 2 – co-design workshops (3 sessions, 8-10 participants each) with clinicians, developers, and users to translate themes into design requirements; Phase 3 – pilot RCT (n=120, 80% power, α=0.05) comparing feedback-informed vs. standard CDSS, with outcomes adherence (app logins), trust (Likert scale), and symptom reduction (PHQ-9/GAD-7) at 8 weeks, plus qualitative interviews (n=20) to explore mechanisms. Novelty lies in leveraging informal LLM feedback via a formal design framework, extending beyond static ethical guidelines (Paper 3) and addressing the lack of user feedback integration (Paper 1, 4). Expected contributions include a validated feedback integration framework and preliminary efficacy evidence. Limitations: social media feedback may not generalize to clinical populations; small sample size for subgroup analyses; 8-week follow-up may not capture long-term adherence.
draft_proposal: AI tools, particularly large language models (LLMs) and clinical decision support systems (CDSS), are increasingly deployed in mental health support, offering benefits in accessibility and symptom reduction but raising concerns about privacy, bias, and lack of clinical oversight. Ethical frameworks advocate for human-centered, explainable, and supervised integration, yet gaps persist in long-term outcomes, user feedback integration, and robust evaluation. While foundational work on generative information retrieval highlights potential for tailored content, challenges like hallucination remain. This study addresses the gap: how can user feedback from informal AI mental health tools (e.g., LLMs) be systematically integrated into the design of clinically validated, ethical AI systems to improve therapeutic outcomes and user trust? We hypothesize that integrating user feedback from informal LLM interactions into a structured feedback loop for a clinically supervised CDSS will improve treatment adherence and user trust compared to a CDSS without such feedback integration. A mixed-methods design is proposed: Phase 1 involves thematic analysis of user feedback from social media (e.g., TikTok comments) on LLM-based mental health tools, coding for benefits, concerns, and suggestions. Phase 2 employs co-design workshops with clinicians, AI developers, and users to translate themes into design requirements for a CDSS. The CDSS will be prototyped and evaluated in a small-scale pilot RCT (n=60) comparing a feedback-informed CDSS vs. standard CDSS, measuring adherence, trust (Likert scale), and symptom reduction (PHQ-9/GAD-7) at 4 weeks. Expected contributions include a validated framework for integrating user feedback into ethical AI design and preliminary evidence on its impact on clinical outcomes. This proposal extends existing literature by moving beyond static ethical guidelines to a dynamic, user-informed design process, directly addressing the gap in systematic feedback integration noted in prior work.

proposal_critique.clarity_issues: The problem definition is clear but could be more precise: 'systematically integrate user feedback' is vague. Specify what 'systematic integration' entails (e.g., feedback loops, iterative design).
proposal_critique.logic_issues: The transition from Phase 1 (thematic analysis of social media) to Phase 2 (co-design workshops) is logical, but the link to the pilot RCT is weak: how exactly are themes translated into design requirements? The causal chain from feedback integration to improved adherence/trust is assumed but not justified.
proposal_critique.novelty_issues: The gap is well-identified, but the proposed solution (feedback-informed CDSS) is not clearly differentiated from existing user-centered design approaches. The novelty lies in using informal LLM feedback, but this is incremental; stronger justification needed.
proposal_critique.methodology_issues: Feasibility concerns: n=60 is small for an RCT; 4-week follow-up is too short for adherence/trust measurement. Thematic analysis of TikTok comments may not generalize to clinical populations. Co-design workshops require careful recruitment and facilitation.
proposal_critique.literature_alignment_issues: The proposal aligns with Theme 1 (user perspectives, ethical governance) but underutilizes Theme 2 (generative IR) – e.g., retrieval-augmented generation could inform feedback integration. The gap is derived from literature but not explicitly linked to limitations of specific papers.
proposal_critique.academic_depth_issues: The proposal lacks theoretical grounding (e.g., user engagement theory, trust models). The mixed-methods design is described superficially; details on coding reliability, workshop structure, and statistical power are missing.
proposal_critique.revision_plan: Strengthen the theoretical framework by incorporating user engagement and trust models. Expand the methodology: justify sample size with power analysis, extend follow-up to 8-12 weeks, and add a qualitative component to explore mechanisms. Clarify how Phase 1 themes directly inform CDSS design requirements, perhaps using a formal framework like the Double Diamond design process. Explicitly connect the gap to limitations in Papers 1, 3, and 4.

rubric_scores.justification: The research problem is clearly defined: integrating user feedback from informal LLM interactions into clinically validated CDSS. Motivation, background, target users, and proposed solution are exceptionally clear. The proposal explicitly discusses the gap (lack of user feedback integration) and expected contribution (a feedback integration framework). Implications for therapeutic outcomes and trust are well articulated.

The proposal stages (literature analysis, gap identification, hypothesis, mixed-methods design, evaluation) are logically connected and mutually supportive. The reasoning chain from literature gaps to hypothesis to methodology is coherent, with clear inputs/outputs between phases. Transitions are well explained, e.g., how Phase 1 thematic analysis informs Phase 2 co-design.

The proposal presents a distinct research angle: systematically leveraging informal LLM feedback via a formal design framework (Double Diamond) to inform clinically validated CDSS design. This extends beyond static ethical guidelines (Paper 3) and addresses the lack of user feedback integration highlighted in Papers 1 and 4. The contribution is specific (validated framework and preliminary efficacy evidence) and well justified.

The project is realistic with clear datasets (TikTok comments), baselines (standard CDSS), evaluation metrics (adherence, trust, PHQ-9/GAD-7), and implementation plan (phases, sample sizes, power analysis). Risks (generalizability, small sample) are acknowledged. However, details on CDSS prototype development and resource requirements (e.g., developer time) could be more specific.

The proposal is strongly grounded in the retrieved papers. It accurately summarizes relevant literature (Papers 1-5), identifies gaps (user feedback integration, lack of user-centered design), and explains how the proposal extends prior work (e.g., beyond static guidelines in Paper 3). Critical comparison is clear and supports the research direction.

The proposal demonstrates mature academic thinking: verifiable assumptions (e.g., feedback improves trust), theoretical awareness (Double Diamond design process), methodological rigor (mixed-methods, inter-coder reliability, power analysis), and limitation awareness (generalizability, follow-up duration). It moves beyond summarization to research-level insight.

Writing is clear, concise, and professional. Sections are well organized, terminology is consistent, and the proposal is easy to follow. Citations are appropriately used. No issues with formatting or academic tone.

evaluation.comments: Overall, the proposal is strong across all criteria, with clear problem definition, logical coherence, high novelty, feasible design, strong literature alignment, academic depth, and excellent presentation. Minor improvements could include more detailed resource planning for the CDSS prototype.
